picks.why: The Peyraud family estate at Le Plan du Castellet that built Bandol's name on Mourvèdre; La Tourtine, its structured parcel red from a limestone slope, is the wine that teaches Bandol rouge.
picks.note: Confirm La Tourtine's Mourvèdre share in words, its slope and the first vintage bottled apart from the domaine's own page or two sources; Cabassaou, La Migoua and the rosé go in others.

picks.why: The Meyreuil estate of one family that holds most of the small Palette appellation; its white, raised in old foudres from very old vines, is the wine of the appellation.
picks.note: Say the estate's share of Palette only in words that do not age; confirm the white's grapes (Clairette leading, by the library) and its cellars from the estate's page or two sources.

picks.why: The Alpilles estate planted on cleared limestone scrub from 1973, whose red of Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah broke the Baux-de-Provence rule on Cabernet and is sold as IGP Alpilles.
picks.note: Name the founder only with his dates from two sources; confirm the vintage the red left the appellation and the IGP named on the label in the years taught; the white goes in others.

picks.why: The house founded by an Alsatian agronomist who reached Provence in 1896, which helped carry Provence rosé onto wine lists; the rosé of its Château de Selle, in the house's curved bottle, is the wine to know.
picks.note: Confirm the label words (Château de Selle, Cœur de Grain) and the date and story of the curved bottle in two sources; give the founder's dates from two sources; Clos Mireille and Château Romassan go in others; later ownership is history, dated.

picks.why: The La Motte-en-Provence estate behind Whispering Angel, the Côtes de Provence rosé guests ask for by name; Garrus, its oak-fermented rosé, is the estate's other face.
picks.note: The buyer of 2006 is living: name him by role only. Say where Whispering Angel's fruit comes from only in the estate's own words; Garrus and Rock Angel go in others.

picks.why: The Aniane estate of 1971 whose Cabernet Sauvignon-led red, first made in the late 1970s on a pocket of glacial soil, argued that the Languedoc could make wine to age, sold outside the appellations.
picks.note: Confirm the first vintage (1978 by most accounts), the founders' dates and the label's Vin de Pays, now IGP, from the estate's history page; the soil story is the estate's own, told as such.

picks.producer: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
picks.why: Aniane's other estate, founded in 1992, whose red of Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cabernet Sauvignon is aged long in barrel and sold as IGP Pays d'Hérault.
picks.note: The founder is living and is never named; confirm the grapes in words and the IGP on the label; the white goes in others.

picks.why: The Jonquières estate of 1985 that helped give the Terrasses du Larzac its name; Autour de Jonquières, its principal red, is a blend of the hill's Mediterranean grapes.
picks.note: The founder is living and is never named; confirm the red's grapes and the appellation on its label (Terrasses du Larzac, older vintages Coteaux du Languedoc) in two sources.

picks.why: The Calce estate on limestone and schist in the Agly valley that put dry Roussillon from old vines on wine lists; Muntada, its red from the oldest vines, is the estate's flagship.
picks.note: The family is living and is never named; confirm Muntada's grapes and its label (IGP Côtes Catalanes or Côtes du Roussillon Villages) in the vintages taught; Coume Gineste goes in others.

picks.why: The Maury estate known for vin doux naturel of Grenache left first in glass bonbonnes in the sun and then for years in old casks; the ten year old shows that oxidative style in full.
picks.note: Confirm the present label of the aged Maury (10 Ans d'Âge, or its successor) and the steps of bonbonne and cask from the estate's page; the Vintage and the Maury Sec go in others.

picks.why: The Château-Chalon family estate whose vin jaune, Savagnin aged untopped under its veil of yeast and released in the 62 cl clavelin, is the wine a sommelier is taught to place.
picks.note: Confirm the family's dates before naming anyone; give the vin jaune rule from the appellation text (sixty months untopped by the region record); the Côtes du Jura Blanc goes in others.

picks.why: The Pupillin estate whose Ploussard, a pale red made with little or no added sulphur, became a bottle the natural wine movement looks to; it teaches the Jura's own red grape.
picks.note: The grower whose name the house bears and his successor are living: name neither in prose, say the founder and his successor. Confirm the label and the sulphur custom in two sources.

picks.why: The Montigny-lès-Arsures family estate that makes every Jura style; Les Bruyères, a topped-up, single-vineyard Chardonnay, shows the fresh idiom beside the oxidative one.
picks.note: The son who runs it is living and is never named; confirm Les Bruyères's soil and élevage and any biodynamic farming with its year in two sources; the vin jaune and the Crémant go in others.

picks.why: The historic château estate of the Côtes du Jura at Arlay, long a reference for vin jaune and vin de paille; its vin de paille, from grapes dried for months before pressing, is the sweet face of the region.
picks.note: Confirm the label (Côtes du Jura Vin de Paille), its grapes and the drying from the estate or two sources; the family is living and is never named; the vin jaune goes in others.

picks.why: The Arbois estate founded in 2012 by a family of Volnay, bottling Savagnin topped up, beside its vin jaune; the ouillé Savagnin shows the grape without the veil.
picks.note: Name the Volnay family by its domaine, never its living members (one is in people.json); say which vines it took on only from two sources; the vin jaune goes in others.

picks.why: The château on Lake Geneva at Thonon-les-Bains whose vineyard gives the Chasselas cru of Ripaille its name; its white teaches Savoie's lakeside Chasselas.
picks.note: Confirm the label (Vin de Savoie Ripaille), the grape and the château's history under the Dukes of Savoy from the château's page or two sources; the owning family is living and is never named.

picks.why: A family estate at Arbin in the Combe de Savoie whose Mondeuse from the cru of Arbin is a clear way to teach Savoie's own red grape.
picks.note: Confirm the cuvée's exact name (Arbin Mondeuse, or a named bottling such as Vieilles Vignes) and the estate's dates in two sources; the couple who run it are living and are never named in prose.

picks.why: The estate begun in 1998 to replant the abandoned schist slopes of Cevins in the Tarentaise, bottled as IGP Vin des Allobroges; Quartz, its Altesse, is the white to know.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year, Quartz as Altesse alone and the IGP on its label; the founder and those who run it now are living and are never named.

picks.why: A family estate at Aimavigne in Jongieux at the foot of the Marestel slope, known for long-lived Altesse from the cru; its Marestel shows what the grape becomes with age.
picks.note: Confirm the family's generations and any custom of late release only in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: A family estate at Mérignat in the Bugey known for Cerdon, the pink, sweetish sparkling wine of Gamay and Poulsard made by the ancestral method, its fermentation finished in the bottle.
picks.note: Confirm the label (Bugey Cerdon, méthode ancestrale) and that the blend moves from year to year; the family is living and is never named.

picks.why: The Vire-sur-Lot estate whose Le Cèdre, Malbec from old vines on the terraces and the stony ground above, aged long in oak, set the modern face of Cahors.
picks.note: The brothers who made its name are living and are never named; confirm Le Cèdre's soils, élevage and the family's dates in two sources; the château wine goes in others.

picks.why: The Madiran estate whose pure Tannat raised in new oak lifted the appellation's name from the 1980s; the Cuvée Prestige, from old vines on stony slopes, is the wine that did it.
picks.note: The library holds the wine too (w-montus-cuvee-prestige): agree with it. Confirm the cuvée's present label (Prestige, or XL for the longer élevage) and its first vintage; the founder is living and is never named.

picks.why: The Monein estate that is a reference for Jurançon, dry and sweet; Quintessence, Petit Manseng picked very late from berries shrivelled on the vine, shows that Jurançon's sweetness is passerillage, not noble rot.
picks.note: Confirm the picking dates and élevage of Quintessence from the estate or two sources; the founder is living and is never named; Chant des Vignes goes in others.

picks.why: The Monbazillac estate taken on in 1992 that showed the appellation could make botrytised wine to set beside Sauternes; Cuvée Madame, a berry by berry selection made only when the year allows, is its flagship.
picks.note: The couple who took it on are living and are never named; confirm the lease of 1992, the years Cuvée Madame was made and its grapes in words (Muscadelle and Sémillon) in two sources.

picks.why: The Gaillac family estate that keeps the old local grapes in the vineyard; its Mauzac Nature, sparkling by the ancestral method with its fermentation finished in bottle, teaches the old Gaillac way with bubbles.
picks.note: Confirm the method and the label (Gaillac Mauzac Nature) and the generations of the family in two sources; the living family is never named; the Vin de Voile goes in others.

picks.why: The Figari estate on southern granite whose red of the island's own grapes is a reference for the revival of Corsica's old varieties.
picks.note: Confirm the red's grapes (Sciaccarello and Nielluccio by report) and its label (Corse Figari) in two sources; the grower is living and is never named; the Biancu Gentile goes in others.

picks.why: The Patrimonio family estate on limestone whose Vermentino from the Carco parcel shows how long the island's white can live.
picks.note: The founder and his sons are living: the house keeps its name, none is named in prose. Confirm Carco as Vermentino from one parcel; Grotte di Sole, the red, goes in others.

picks.why: The Taravo valley estate near Ajaccio, farmed biodynamically, that keeps a collection of the island's old grapes; Faustine, its Ajaccio red of Sciaccarello, is the estate's appellation range.
picks.note: Confirm Faustine's appellation (Ajaccio) and grapes; the Cuvées Collection are Vin de France and go in others; the general the house is named for may be named only with dates from two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: An estate at Rogliano at the northern tip of Cap Corse, on schist, known for its Vermentino and its Muscat du Cap Corse, the vin doux naturel of Muscat à Petits Grains.
picks.note: Confirm the Muscat's label name (Muscatellu by one guide) and whether the white, Corse Coteaux du Cap Corse, is better known; the family is living and is never named.

picks.why: A family estate of Patrimonio on limestone, a clear example of Nielluccio, the grape DNA ties to Sangiovese, in the island's northern appellation.
picks.note: Confirm the red's cuvée name (Petra Bianca by report) and that it is Nielluccio led; Domaine Leccia is the family estate, not Domaine d'E Croce, which a member of the family founded apart; the living family is never named.

picks.why: The Melgaço family estate that bottled the first Alvarinho of the municipality in 1982, by its own account, and whose Alvarinho carried the subregion's grape abroad.
picks.note: Hedge the 1982 first as the family's claim, from the estate's page; the living family is never named; Primeiras Vinhas and Granit go in others.

picks.why: The Monção manor whose varietal Alvarinho, sold from the 1970s, made the grape's name in Portugal before most growers bottled it.
picks.note: Confirm the first vintage (1976 by report), the manor's building and its purchase in 1937 in two sources; name the woman who planted the Alvarinho only if two sources give her dates and her death.

picks.why: The Melgaço house of a winemaker who showed Alvarinho could take lees, skin contact and oak; Muros Antigos is its wide release Alvarinho, the bottle a list carries.
picks.note: The founder is living: the house keeps its name and he is never named in prose. Confirm Muros Antigos's making; Curtimenta and Parcela Única go in others.

picks.why: The Penafiel house of the Guedes family behind Casal Garcia, launched in 1939, the light, lightly sparkling Vinho Verde that carried the region's name abroad.
picks.note: Confirm the 1939 launch and the blend in words (Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto and Azal by report) from Aveleda's page; the family's living members are never named.

picks.why: The Lima valley estate that showed Loureiro, the Lima's own grape, could be made seriously and age; Esporão bought it in 2019.
picks.note: Confirm the label (Quinta do Ameal Loureiro, Ameal Loureiro since 2019) and the estate's history before 2019 in two sources; the former owner is living and is never named; the Reserva of the Marinhas plot goes in others.

picks.why: A family estate at Abrunhosa do Mato between Mangualde and Nelas whose varietal Touriga Nacional and barrel-fermented Encruzado helped define the modern Dão in the 1990s.
picks.note: Confirm the first varietal Touriga Nacional and its year in two sources; the family is living and is never named; the Encruzado goes in others.

picks.why: The old-vine estate under the Serra da Estrela near Seia, with its sister Quinta de Saes, whose fine-boned reds argue for the Dão's elegance; Carrocel, its Touriga Nacional from old vines, is the estate's flagship.
picks.note: The library's record is Álvaro Castro (Quinta da Pellada and Quinta de Saes): the winemaker is living, so the house is named by its estate and he is never named in prose. Confirm Carrocel's label and grapes; Primus and Pape go in others, Pape without its living partner's name.

picks.why: Sogrape's Dão estate at Mangualde and a reference for Encruzado, the Dão's white grape, fermented partly in new oak; Único, the estate's red, is its other face.
picks.note: Confirm the Encruzado's making from Sogrape's own sheet and the year Sogrape took the estate in two sources; Único goes in others.

picks.why: The historic manor of Santar near Nelas, among the first houses to bottle estate Dão; its Reserva red of Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz is the wine a list carries.
picks.note: Sources disagree on the manor's age (sixteenth to eighteenth century): leave founded empty unless two agree; confirm the early estate bottling and the Reserva's grapes in words; the Condessa de Santar white goes in others.

picks.why: A nineteenth century estate at Passarella near Gouveia under the Serra da Estrela, revived with its old vines; Villa Oliveira, its Touriga Nacional from an old vineyard, is its flagship red.
picks.note: Confirm the building of 1892 (one source) and the age of the Villa Oliveira vineyard in two sources; those who revived it are living and are never named; the Villa Oliveira Encruzado goes in others.

picks.why: The Anadia house that championed Baga from the 1980s with single-vineyard wines; Vinha Barrosa, from old bush vines, is the traditional face of the grape, and the ungrafted Pé Franco on sand its rarity.
picks.note: The founder is living: the house keeps its name and he is never named in prose. Confirm Vinha Barrosa's soils and the label's category (Vinho Regional, the house having left the DOC, by report); the Pé Franco and Vinha Pan go in others.

picks.why: The Bairrada merchant house founded in 1920 by the Costa brothers, whose Frei João reds, kept for years in its cellars before release, showed how long Baga could live.
picks.note: Name the brothers only with dates from two sources; confirm which Frei João to teach (Reserva or Garrafeira) and its grapes; Porta dos Cavaleiros, the house's Dão, goes in others.

picks.why: A family estate near Anadia making Baga the old way, in lagar and old wood, and sparkling wine with long lees ageing; its Garrafeira red is the classic Bairrada to know.
picks.note: Confirm the Garrafeira's label and making in two sources; the family is living and is never named; the sparkling wines go in others.

picks.why: A Sangalhos estate making Baga in the old manner, trodden in lagar and aged in old wood, whose Garrafeira red shows the slow-ageing classic style of the region.
picks.note: Confirm the estate's history and dates and the Garrafeira's making in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: The palace hotel in the Buçaco forest whose red and white, blended from Bairrada and Dão grapes and aged for years before release, are sold as table wine outside both appellations.
picks.note: Confirm the label words (Buçaco Tinto Reservado, Vinho de Mesa) and the old cellar's vintages in two sources; the hotel's family and any living winemaker or partner are never named.

picks.why: The co-operative founded in 1931 that keeps Colares alive, ageing Ramisco from ungrafted vines in the sand by the sea in old vats for years before release.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year and any claim of Portugal's oldest wine co-operative only in two sources; confirm Arenae's label (Colares, Ramisco) and its ageing.

picks.why: A Colares house dating from 1808 by its own account, whose cellar of old vintages shows how Ramisco from the sand ages over decades.
picks.note: Hedge 1808 as the house's claim and confirm the red's label wording (Colares, Ramisco) in two sources; the living owners are never named; the Malvasia white goes in others.

picks.why: The Bucelas estate whose Prova Régia, all Arinto, made the white-only appellation's grape known abroad; the name recalls royal approval.
picks.note: One listing gives Sogrape as the maker: confirm who has made Prova Régia and since when before writing ownership; the estate is spelled Romeyra on some labels; Morgado de Santa Catherina goes in others.

picks.why: The project of the Oeiras municipal council that brought Carcavelos, the fortified wine of the coast west of Lisbon, back from near extinction, and almost the only maker of the appellation.
picks.note: Confirm the project's start, the vineyard it farms and the ages on its labels in two sources; the Marquis of Pombal (1699 to 1782) may be named with his dates.

picks.why: The Alenquer estate that proved Syrah belongs in Lisboa; its Reserva, Syrah with a little Viognier in the manner of the northern Rhône, is the house's flagship.
picks.note: Sources disagree on the estate's start (bought in 1987 with a first wine in 1997, or founded in 1990): leave founded empty unless two agree; the founder is living and is never named.

picks.why: An Almeirim estate dating from 1723, named for a marquisate won in India, and one of the Tejo's oldest names; the Marquesa de Alorna Grande Reserva is its flagship range.
picks.note: Confirm 1723 and the marquisate's story from the estate or two sources; the Grande Reserva is made red and white, so the author names the colour taught and its grapes.

picks.why: An old family estate at Almeirim whose Falcoaria label, named for the house's falconry, carries the Tejo's firmer reds of traditional grapes and oak-aged whites.
picks.note: Confirm the falconry story and which Falcoaria to teach (the red, or the Grande Reserva) in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: The Muge estate on the left bank of the Tejo, held by one family for centuries, whose Marquesa de Cadaval red is its flagship.
picks.note: Confirm the founding (1648 by one retailer) and the family's history in two sources; labels write de or do Cadaval and a white of the name exists, so name the red's grapes only as the estate states them; the Trincadeira Preta goes in others.

picks.why: A large estate at Alpiarça on the south bank that grows Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Syrah beside horses and cork; its Grande Escolha reds, bottled by grape, show the modern Tejo on one farm.
picks.note: The Grande Escolha is bottled as Syrah and as Alfrocheiro: choose one and name it whole on the record from the estate's sheet; the Dona Isabel Juliana sparkling goes in others.

picks.why: The farm company of the floodplain founded in 1836, whose winery at Catapereiro on the Charneca sand shows what the south bank can do when yields are held down; its 1836 range carries the founding year.
picks.note: Confirm the 1836 range's label and colour (a Grande Reserva white is recorded) in two sources; the Tyto Alba range, from vines in the estuary's nature reserve, goes in others.

picks.why: The Azeitão house founded in 1834 that made Moscatel de Setúbal its name, its Moscatel brand dating from 1849 by its own timeline; Alambre is its Moscatel, and Periquita, of 1850, its red.
picks.note: Not the Port house of the same name. Confirm which Alambre to teach (the young one or the 20 Anos) and the Torna Viagem story from the house's own pages; Periquita goes in others.

picks.why: The Azeitão company, once J.P. Vinhos, named for the palace and estate of Bacalhôa, whose Quinta da Bacalhôa, a red of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, is its flagship.
picks.note: Confirm the first vintage of the Quinta da Bacalhôa red and the vineyard's planting from the company or two sources; the company's living owner is never named; the Moscatels and Palácio da Bacalhôa go in others.

picks.why: A family estate at Fernando Pó on the Palmela sand, dating from 1920 by report, that built its name on Castelão; Dona Ermelinda is its Palmela red.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year, the Dona Ermelinda red's appellation (Palmela) and its grapes in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: A family house of the peninsula dating from 1910 by report, credited with bringing back Moscatel Roxo, the pink-skinned Muscat once near lost, as fortified Moscatel de Setúbal.
picks.note: Confirm 1910 and the revival claim in two sources, and the label (Moscatel de Setúbal Roxo and its age statement); the living family is never named.

picks.why: The co-operative of the Pegões plain, the everyday voice of the peninsula's wine; its Colheita Seleccionada, made red and white, is its widely seen label.
picks.note: Confirm the colour taught (the white is Fernão Pires, Antão Vaz, Verdelho, Arinto and Chardonnay by one sheet), the co-operative's full name and founding; its Moscatel goes in others.

picks.why: The traditional Alentejo in one estate: Alicante Bouschet planted since the nineteenth century, trodden in stone lagares and aged in old wood; Mouchão, its red made only in accepted years, lasts for decades.
picks.note: Name members of the founding family only with dates from two sources; confirm the years Mouchão was not made; Tonel 3-4 goes in others.

picks.why: The Évora foundation that makes wine at Cartuxa beside the Carthusian monastery that named it, and bottles Pêra-Manca red only in the years it judges fit.
picks.note: Name the founder only with dates from two sources; confirm the red's first vintage and tell the older story of the Pêra-Manca name as legend where it is one; Cartuxa Reserva goes in others.

picks.why: The Reguengos estate whose winery of the 1980s led the Alentejo's modern revival; its Reserva red is one of the region's widely known wines.
picks.note: Confirm the founding, the first Reserva vintage and the red's grapes in words in two sources; the founding family is living and is never named; the white Reserva goes in others.

picks.why: The co-operative of the marble country, founded in 1955, whose Reserva red with its cork label taught a generation of Portuguese what an Alentejo red tastes like.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year and the cork label (rótulo de cortiça) in two sources, and the Reserva's grapes in words.

picks.why: A Vidigueira estate whose Syrah, first released in 1998, could not be named for its grape under the rules of the day and was sold as Incógnito; Syrah has since been admitted.
picks.note: Confirm 1998 and the year of the rule change in two sources; the founders are living and are never named; the label is Vinho Regional Alentejano.
